prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated in large numbers on a narrow optical transition, bringing frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B030 to B012 (Katori and Ye) as the sole prize part. The change rests on specific arguments from round 1, not on the count of supporters. First, my novelty worry was that the 2005 comb prize and Wineland's 2012 prize already cover this territory. Kroll, Pearce, Olsson and Lindroth made the same point from different angles and I now accept it: the comb measures optical frequencies and the 2012 work controls single quantum systems, whereas the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate idea, state-independent trapping that cancels the light shift so that thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil shifts. That is what moved stability and accuracy together, and a citation worded around the lattice and many-atom interrogation says so. Second, I treated the pending redefinition of the second as leaving the impact unfinished. I now think it is a consequence of the achievement and not a precondition: 10^-18 uncertainty is reproduced in several laboratories, and relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants already exist. Third, my own B030 case has weakened on reflection. The omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, with Zhang deceased, and of the three-dimensional work is more than a wording problem under a three-name limit, and the 2016 prize on topological phases of matter makes the topic look less new than I first argued. By contrast the Katori and Ye pairing is the cleanest attribution on the list: concept and first strontium lattice clock, and the push to record accuracy and coherence. My preference for conceptual advances over instruments remains, but I no longer think it separates B030 from B012 enough to outweigh these points. Because the other credit and timing issues are settled by wording, one prize part is enough, and I see no second part that could be allocated fairly under the three-person cap.
statement.case_against: I do not think the credit objection to B012 disappears. Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, and the strontium versus ytterbium first-demonstration history, are outside the two names, and I cannot verify that history from the files, as several colleagues also say. If it turned out that the first lattice-clock demonstration was substantially due to others, a two-name prize would be harder to defend. The ion-clock lineage reaches comparable uncertainty, so the citation must rest on the lattice concept and not on accuracy in general. It also remains true that B012 is an instrument achievement and B030 and B042 changed how classes of materials are understood. B042 has the larger recent scientific footprint, and I would put it first if the field's superconducting mechanism were settled and its credit among Cao, Dean, Young, Efetov and others could be resolved within three names.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the comb prize recognised the measurement of optical frequencies and the 2012 prize the control of single quantum systems, whereas the magic-wavelength lattice is a different idea, state-independent trapping of many atoms, and that the 10^-18 result is established whatever the General Conference on Weights and Measures decides.
responses.response: This is the argument that moved me most. I had folded the lattice clock into a sequence of metrology steps; Kroll's separation between measuring optical frequencies, controlling one ion and trapping many atoms at a magic wavelength is the right one, and it fits the physics I can follow: the light-shift cancellation is atomic-structure physics, not a refinement of a comb. I also accept his point about a regulatory step. I would keep his candid note that he cannot judge the first-demonstration history, and I ask that the committee not rely on our shared confidence for that history.

responses.point: Pearce accepts that the novelty concern is serious but not decisive, since the magic-wavelength trick moved uncertainties from 10^-16 to 10^-18, and agrees that the citation should say what the lattice clock added and not simply refer to precision timekeeping.
responses.response: I agree with that wording requirement and have written my citation to name the magic-wavelength trapping and many-atom interrogation. Pearce also concedes that B042 has the larger recent scientific footprint, which I share, but a larger footprint is not the same as a settled attribution, and his own file now doubts the Bistritzer and Cao credit. That is why I no longer ask for B042 as lead this year.

responses.point: Olsson argues that the redefinition of the second is a consequence of the achievement and not a precondition, and she ranks B030 sixth, regarding attribution incompleteness as weighing heavily.
responses.response: I accept the point on the redefinition and have dropped it as a maturity condition. In round 1 I asked whether her sixth place for B030 was decisive on attribution; after rereading, I think she and Kroll are right that the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and of the three-dimensional work is more serious than I allowed, and I no longer say a citation naming HgTe fixes it. I still think the experimental half, the observation of the quantum spin Hall state, is real physics, and I would keep B030 as a candidate for a later year.

responses.point: Mehlig names the open tension that an instrument achievement is arguably less of a physics discovery than a conceptual advance such as topological band theory, and notes that credit in lattice clocks extends to Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow and Lemke.
responses.response: I held the same view in round 1, and I do not claim it is wrong, only that it does not separate these candidates enough once B030's credit gap is counted. The magic-wavelength lattice is a concept as well as a device: it changes what can be done with atomic structure. On credit, Mehlig is right that the citation must be worded to avoid re-rewarding the comb and ion-control lineages, and I would favour a citation that names the lattice and many-atom interrogation and leaves others' demonstrations to the scientific background. His round-1 question to me on finite-dimensional failures of DMFT is now moot for my preference, but my answer was that nonlocal correlations and the contested 1989 and 1992 credit are the real limits.

responses.point: Johansson asked what made the lattice clock an eighth-place achievement for me, and whether the earlier metrology prizes were the reason, and he asks that the citation not rest on accuracy in general.
responses.response: My eighth place was mainly distance from my own field and the weight I gave the earlier prizes, and I accept that this was not a scientific judgement on merit. I agree with his caution on accuracy: ion clocks reach comparable uncertainty, so the citation should rest on the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation, which is what neither the comb nor single-ion control provides. His timing concern about B005 after the 2025 prize I share, and I do not propose it or B020 this year.

uncertainties: Whether Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, and the strontium versus ytterbium first-demonstration history, make a Katori and Ye pairing unfair; I cannot verify this and would want it checked before a final vote.

Whether the citation can convey the lattice concept and many-atom interrogation clearly enough to separate the work from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or whether a critic would still see a third metrology prize.
Whether my change from B030 reflects the evidence or the weight of an eight-member discussion. I think the specific arguments carry it, but I cannot fully exclude drift toward consensus.
Whether B042 becomes a better lead once the superconducting mechanism is settled and the Bistritzer and Cao, Dean, Young and Efetov credit can be resolved within three names.
statement.conflict_note: I keep my earlier disclosure: dynamical mean-field theory (B008) and LDA+DMFT are methods on my Uppsala profile and I ranked B008 first in the opening ballot, so I will not advocate it and would consider recusing from any vote on it. It is no longer my preferred part. My profile lists no personal or institutional link to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer, and publicly documented ties (my doctoral supervisor Börje Johansson, Los Alamos, Uppsala colleagues) do not indicate any. I have no new disclosure.
